title: The Habitable Zone
objective: After this level you can explain the habitable zone and why liquid water matters.
summary: The habitable zone is where a planet could hold liquid water. It sits closer to dim stars; TRAPPIST-1 has planets in its zone.

cards.headline: Not too hot, not too cold. Planets have a Goldilocks zone.
cards.body: Around every star there’s a band where a planet could be just right for liquid water. Where that band sits depends on the star.

cards.headline: Just right for water
cards.body: The habitable zone is the range of distances from a star where a planet’s surface could be the right temperature for liquid water. Where it lies depends on the star. Around dim, cool stars like red dwarfs, the zone sits much closer in; around bright stars, it’s farther out. It’s like a campfire: with a small fire, you pull your chair in close.
cards.callout: Dim star → close zone · Bright star → far zone

cards.headline: Not a guarantee
cards.body: Being in the habitable zone doesn’t guarantee liquid water, let alone life. A planet’s atmosphere matters too. Remember Venus from Level 3? Its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat, and its surface bakes at over 450 °C. The right address doesn’t help if the air is wrong.

cards.context: This red dwarf, about 40 light-years away, is one of the small, cool stars whose habitable zone hugs it closely, and several of its planets sit inside that zone. One dim star, seven Earth-sized worlds, and more than one pulled up close to the campfire.

cards.headline: Habitable zone: mapped
learned: The habitable zone allows liquid surface water
Location isn’t a guarantee: atmospheres matter
TRAPPIST-1 has planets in its zone

questions.prompt: What is a star’s habitable zone?

options.label: The region where a star is born
Where a planet could be the right temperature for liquid water
The part of a star that can be seen
The area where comets form
options.rationale: Comets come from the Kuiper Belt and Oort Cloud.

questions.explanation: The habitable zone is the range of distances where a planet’s surface could hold liquid water.

questions.prompt: Why is the habitable zone around a red dwarf so close to the star?

options.label: Red dwarfs are dim and cool, so planets must be close to stay warm
Red dwarfs have stronger gravity
options.rationale: Gravity isn’t what sets the zone.

options.label: Red dwarfs are bigger than the Sun
Red dwarfs have no planets far away
options.rationale: The zone is set by warmth.

questions.explanation: A dim star gives off little heat, so the zone where water could stay liquid lies close to it.

questions.prompt: From Level 3: Venus sits near the inner edge of the Sun’s habitable zone. Why isn’t it habitable?

options.label: It is too far from the Sun
It has no atmosphere
options.rationale: It has a very thick one.

options.label: Its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps too much heat

questions.explanation: Venus’s thick atmosphere traps heat, pushing its surface over 450 °C. Location alone doesn’t make a planet habitable.
